title: The Justice of the Parrot (简体中文)
summary: In the marketplace of Vijayanagara, two merchants—an honest grain dealer named Madhava and a scheming textile trader named Bhima—appeared... [ZH]
full_text:
In the marketplace of Vijayanagara, two merchants—an honest grain dealer named Madhava and a scheming textile trader named Bhima—appeared before the royal magistrate claiming ownership of an extraordinarily intelligent green parrot.
The bird was capable of reciting verses, greeting customers, and calculating numbers.

Madhava wept: 'Your Honor, I raised this parrot from a fledgling; yesterday it flew out of its cage, and Bhima captured it and refuses to return it!'
Bhima shouted: 'A lie! This bird was hatched in my grandmother's garden, and has lived in my shop for five years!'

Because both men produced witnesses who swore contradictory oaths, the magistrate was baffled and referred the dispute to Tenali Raman.

Tenali had the parrot brought into the courtroom in its gilded cage.
He asked Bhima: 'What does thy parrot eat every morning?'
Bhima answered readily: 'It feeds on roasted pistachios and sweet cream, as befits a wealthy merchant's bird!'
Tenali asked Madhava: 'What does thy parrot eat?'
Madhava replied: 'Simple dry millet, green chilies, and slices of wild guava.'

Tenali then covered the cage with a dark cloth and carried it to his private garden.
He placed two wooden bowls side by side inside the cage: one containing sweet cream and pistachios, the other containing wild guava seeds and fresh green chilies.
The moment the cloth was removed, the parrot turned immediately to the green chili and guava, devouring them with eager chirps while completely ignoring the pistachios!

Next, Tenali instructed the court clerk to stand outside the closed room and drop a metal tray with a loud crash.
When the tray clattered, the parrot squawked in alarm:
*‘Madhava! Madhava! Guard the grain bins! The wind has blown the latch!’*

Tenali smiled and brought the cage back before the assembly.
'The evidence is complete,' declared Tenali. 'A bird raised on pistachios does not prefer guava seeds, and in moments of fright, it calls out the name of the master who fed it for years!'

Confronted with the parrot's own testimony, Bhima confessed his theft.
The bird was restored to Madhava, Bhima was fined thirty silver coins, and the court praised Tenali’s keen understanding that the innocent habits of living creatures cannot be bribed or perjured.
moral: Observation of subtle habits and speech reveals the true owner where false oaths create confusion. [ZH]
